name: Raisin Purple
lede: Raisin Purple is a dark, muted purplish red that Ridgway's 1912 atlas placed at two separate tones on one plate, and that the 1955 dictionary filed as a reddish purple.

sections.title: One name, two tones
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* gives hue 65 on plate XI at tone k for a reading close to this hex [1]. A second reading of the same hue appears nearby at tone i, both read from a scan of an aged printed plate, so both are approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 filed the name under block 242, dark reddish purple, but the swatch measures nearer block 259, dark purplish red, and still 8.0 units off its center, a loose fit either way [1].

Its nearest library neighbors are [[dull-dark-purple|Dull Dark Purple]] at 3.1 units and [[twilight-lavender|Twilight Lavender]] at 3.4, near twins on a screen [1]. Set beside [[raisin-black|Raisin Black]], which carries the same "Raisin" word toward near-total darkness, this one keeps far more visible purple and red [1]. [[rubient|Rubient]], a darker, browner red, measures into the same block 259 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of it covers at least five percent of the canvas in only 7 of our 23,781 archive paintings, as photographed, rarer than 75 percent of our named colors [2]. The earliest dated example is from 1600, and the latest from 1915, across 6 dated paintings total, 312 years before Ridgway's 1912 record, a floor set by thin coverage rather than a true first sighting [2]. In printed English the phrase peaks in use in the 1920s and rises fastest in that same decade, across all senses of the words [2].

Editor spot-audit 2026-10-09: article claimed ISCC-NBS 1955 put it in block 259 shared with Rubient; library src says 1955 block 242 (dark reddish purple); 259 is only the computed nearest centroid, and Rubient has no 1955 entry. Rewrote section, lede, question, opener. Neighbor distances corrected to graph edges (Dull Dark Purple 3.1, Twilight Lavender 3.4).
